steps.text: The Long Map. The Story of the Jews. Cyrus, and the return to Zion.

events.title: Babylon falls, 539 BC
events.text: The Nabonidus Chronicle says that in 539 BC Cyrus fought the army of Akkad at Opis on the Tigris, took Sippar without a battle, and that in the month of Tashritu Ugbaru and the Persian army entered Babylon, also without a battle. Cyrus himself entered a few days later, and peace was imposed. Herodotus, a century later, tells a different tale: that Cyrus diverted the river and came in by a dry bed.
events.why: The chronicle is close to the event and does not mention a diverted river. The two accounts of how the city fell do not agree.
claims: The chronicle: battle at Opis, Sippar taken, Babylon entered in Tashritu 539 BC without a battle.
Herodotus says Cyrus diverted the river and took the city by a dry bed.
The two accounts do not agree.

events.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
events.text: A clay cylinder found in Babylon, now in the British Museum, is inscribed in the name of Cyrus. He speaks as a Babylonian king, says that Marduk chose him and took him into the city without a fight, and that he returned gods to their cities and let displaced people go home and rebuild their temples. The cylinder does not name Judah, Jerusalem, or the god of Israel.
events.why: It is a real court inscription, written in the traditional language of Babylonian kingship, for the cults of Mesopotamia. What it does not say matters as much as what it does.
claims: The Cyrus Cylinder is a real inscription from the court of Cyrus, found in Babylon.
It records a policy of returning cult images and displaced people.
It does not name Judah, Jerusalem, or the god of Israel.

events.title: The decree in Ezra
events.text: The book of Ezra, and the end of Chronicles, say that Cyrus issued a decree: the Lord, the god of heaven, had given him all the kingdoms of the earth and had charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. Some scholars read this as a later memory of the general policy on the cylinder, written in the language of Judah. Others think a specific permission for Jerusalem may have been given, and is now lost.
events.why: The cylinder is attested. The decree in Ezra is a biblical tradition. How the two relate is the open question.
claims: Ezra 1 and 2 Chronicles 36 tell of a decree of Cyrus for a house in Jerusalem.
Whether that decree is a later memory of a general policy, or a lost specific permission, is disputed.

events.title: The return, and a small province
events.text: The Bible says that in the first year of Cyrus, families of Judah and Benjamin rose up to go, and that Sheshbazzar brought back the Temple vessels. It gives a great number of those who returned. Archaeology does not show a sudden flood of people in Judah at this time. The land becomes a small Persian province, later called Yehud, under a governor, paying tax to the great king.
events.why: A return happened; its scale is the disagreement. Many families also stayed in Babylonia, as the Al-Yahudu tablets show for decades under Persian rule.
claims: Ezra describes a return led in part by Sheshbazzar, with a large listed number.
Archaeology shows a small, poor Persian province, not a sudden flood of people.
The size of the first return is disputed.
Judean families stayed in Babylonia under Persian rule.

events.title: Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel
events.text: The Bible names two leaders in these years: Sheshbazzar, who is said to have laid a foundation, and Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, with the priest Jeshua. How the two men relate, and whether both belong to the first years of Cyrus, is disputed. Ezra says neighbours offered to help, were refused, and then worked to stop the building, and that the work ceased for years.
events.why: The quarrel may remember real tension between returnees and those who had remained, or between Jerusalem and Samaria. Scholars do not agree how much of Ezra 4 is of this time.
claims: Ezra names Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel, a grandson of Jehoiachin, with the priest Jeshua.
How the two leaders relate is disputed.
Ezra 4 tells of opposition and a halt; how much is of this time is disputed.

events.title: Darius at Behistun
events.text: Cyrus dies on campaign; his son Cambyses takes Egypt. After a crisis Darius, of another branch of the royal house, takes the throne and cuts a great trilingual inscription on the rock at Behistun, telling how he put down revolts across the empire. Yehud is a small corner of this world, which now stretches from the Aegean to the highlands of Iran.
events.why: The details of Cyrus's death are told in more than one way. The Behistun inscription is Darius's own account of how he came to rule.
claims: Cyrus dies on campaign; Cambyses takes Egypt.
The details of Cyrus's death are told in more than one way.
Darius cuts a trilingual inscription at Behistun after taking the throne.

events.title: The Second Temple
events.text: The books of Haggai and Zechariah present themselves as words spoken in the second year of Darius, urging Zerubbabel and the high priest to finish the house of the Lord. Many scholars accept that setting; it is not independently confirmed on a Persian inscription. Ezra says the work resumes, that a scroll is found at Ecbatana, and that in the sixth year of Darius, usually 516 BC, the house is finished and dedicated with joy. No certain stone of that first Second Temple has been identified.
events.why: The dedication is a biblical tradition. The mount would later be rebuilt on a far greater scale under Herod, and what lies under it is not open to us.
claims: Haggai and Zechariah present themselves as words in the second year of Darius.
Whether that date is historical is not independently confirmed on a Persian inscription.
Ezra 6 says the house was finished in the sixth year of Darius and dedicated.
No certain remains of that first phase have been identified.

events.title: Life in two places
events.text: Yehud is a small Persian province, with a governor, a priest and a tax, not a restored kingdom of David. Coins and seals from a little later name the province and its governors; they do not restore a king. In Babylonia, Judean families still live by the canals, and will for generations. The exile did not simply end. It became a life in two places.
events.why: The Bible remembers a return after seventy years. Seventy years is a round number, counted in more than one way, and archaeology does not show an empty land for seventy years.
claims: Yehud is a small Persian province, not a restored kingdom.
Judean families continued in Babylonia under Persia.
Seventy years is a biblical round number; the land was not empty for seventy years.

steps.text: When Jerusalem fell, the king in Babylon was already on the throne. His name was Nabonidus, and he was not of the old royal house of Nebuchadnezzar.
claims: Nabonidus, not of the old royal house of Nebuchadnezzar, was king in Babylon when Jerusalem fell and after.

steps.text: A Babylonian chronicle says that for years he left the city and dwelt at Teima, in Arabia, and that the New Year festival in Babylon was not held.
claims: Nabonidus spent years at Teima in Arabia, and the New Year festival in Babylon was not held.

steps.text: His son Belshazzar, named in Babylonian texts and later in the Bible, ruled in the city in his father's place.
claims: Belshazzar, son of Nabonidus, is named in Babylonian texts and ruled in the city in his father's place.
The book of Daniel also names Belshazzar, in a later story.

steps.text: The book of Daniel tells of a feast in Babylon, and of writing on the wall. That story is later tradition, not a chronicle of the fall.
claims: The feast and the writing on the wall in Daniel 5 are later tradition.

steps.text: In the east, a Persian king was already taking land. In his own inscriptions he is Cyrus, king of Anshan, of the house called Achaemenid.
claims: Cyrus, king of Anshan, of the Achaemenid house, was taking land in the east.

steps.text: The Babylonian chronicle says that Cyrus first made war on the Medes, and took their land, whose capital was at Ecbatana.
claims: Cyrus made war on the Medes and took their land, whose capital was at Ecbatana.

steps.text: Greek writers later tell how he took Lydia too, in the west, and its king Croesus, at Sardis. That western campaign is told as Greek tradition.
claims: Cyrus's campaign against Lydia and Croesus is told as Greek tradition by Herodotus.

steps.text: In Babylon, some of the priests of Marduk were unhappy. Nabonidus had favoured the moon god of Harran, and had stayed away from their city.
claims: Nabonidus favoured the moon god of Harran and stayed away from Babylon, to the anger of some of Marduk's priests.

steps.text: A Babylonian text written after the fall, the Verse Account of Nabonidus, accuses the king of neglect and heresy. It is a hostile source, composed under the new regime.
claims: The Verse Account of Nabonidus is a hostile Babylonian text, written after the fall, accusing the king of neglect and heresy.

steps.text: In five thirty nine BC, Cyrus moves west. At Opis on the Tigris, the chronicle says, he met the army of Akkad, and the people of Akkad retreated.
claims: In 539 BC, at Opis on the Tigris, Cyrus met the army of Akkad, and the people of Akkad retreated.
steps.display: In 539 BC, Cyrus moves west. At Opis on the Tigris, the chronicle says, he met the army of Akkad, and the people of Akkad retreated.

steps.text: Then Sippar was taken without a battle. And in the month of Tashritu, Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, and the army of Cyrus entered Babylon, the chronicle says, without a battle.
claims: Sippar was taken without a battle, and in Tashritu Ugbaru and the army of Cyrus entered Babylon without a battle.

steps.text: Imagine the great gates opening, and a foreign army walking in, and the city still standing.
Cyrus himself entered the city a few days later, the chronicle says, and peace was imposed upon it.
claims: Cyrus entered Babylon a few days later, and peace was imposed upon the city.

steps.text: Herodotus, writing a century later, tells a different tale: that Cyrus diverted the river and came in by a dry bed. That is a Greek story, not what the chronicle says.
claims: Herodotus says Cyrus diverted the river and took Babylon by a dry bed.
The Babylonian chronicle says the city was entered without a battle, and does not tell of a diverted river.
The two accounts of how the city fell do not agree.

steps.text: In the ruins of Babylon, more than two thousand years later, a clay cylinder was found, inscribed in the name of Cyrus.
claims: A clay cylinder inscribed in the name of Cyrus was found in the ruins of Babylon.
steps.display: In the ruins of Babylon, more than 2,000 years later, a clay cylinder was found, inscribed in the name of Cyrus.

steps.text: On it, Cyrus speaks as a Babylonian king. He says that Marduk, the great god of the city, searched the lands for a righteous ruler, chose him, and took him into Babylon without a fight.
claims: On the cylinder, Cyrus says that Marduk chose him and took him into Babylon without a fight.

steps.text: He says he returned the gods to their cities, and gathered people who had been settled far from home, and let them go back, and rebuild their temples.
claims: The cylinder says Cyrus returned cult images to their cities and allowed displaced people to go home and rebuild their temples.

steps.text: The cylinder does not name Judah, or Jerusalem, or the god of Israel. What it records is a policy, told in the language of Babylon, for the cults of Mesopotamia.
claims: The Cyrus Cylinder does not name Judah, Jerusalem, or the god of Israel.

steps.text: The Hebrew Bible tells a more specific story. In the book of Ezra, and at the end of Chronicles, Cyrus issues a decree: the Lord, the god of heaven, has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem.
claims: Ezra 1 and 2 Chronicles 36 say Cyrus issued a decree that the Lord charged him to build a house in Jerusalem.

steps.text: Some scholars read that biblical decree as a later memory of the general policy, written in the language of Judah. Others think a specific permission for Jerusalem may have been given, and is now lost.
claims: Whether Ezra's decree is a later memory of a general policy, or a lost specific permission for Jerusalem, is disputed.

steps.text: What we can say is this. The cylinder is a real inscription from the court of Cyrus. The decree in Ezra is a biblical tradition. Both speak of return, in different voices.
claims: The cylinder is a real inscription from the court of Cyrus.
The decree in Ezra is a biblical tradition.
How the two relate is disputed.

steps.text: The Bible says that in the first year of Cyrus the heads of the families of Judah and Benjamin rose up to go, and that Sheshbazzar, a prince of Judah, brought back the vessels of the Temple.
claims: Ezra says that in the first year of Cyrus, families of Judah and Benjamin rose up to go, and Sheshbazzar brought back the Temple vessels.

steps.text: It gives a great number of those who returned. Archaeology, in the land of Judah, does not show a sudden flood of people at this time. The province that appears under Persia is small, and poor.

Archaeology does not show a sudden flood of people in Judah at this time; the Persian province is small and poor.
The size of the first return is disputed.

steps.text: Many families also stayed in Babylon. The tablets from Al-Yahudu go on for decades: Judeans farming, marrying, and paying taxes, under Persian rule as they had under Babylonian rule.

steps.label: Return from Babylon to Zion (from 538 BC)

steps.text: Imagine a column on the road, not a nation on the march, but families, with donkeys and carts, walking back toward the hills they still called home.
Jerusalem, when they reached it, was not the city of Josiah or of Hezekiah. The walls were down. On the Temple mount, if the old platform could still be seen, it was bare.
claims: Jerusalem in the early Persian period was a much reduced city; the walls of the Iron Age city were down.

steps.text: The Bible says they settled in their towns, and that in the seventh month they gathered in Jerusalem, and built an altar, and offered burnt offerings, though the foundation of the Temple was not yet laid.
claims: Ezra 3 says the returnees built an altar and offered burnt offerings before the Temple foundation was laid.

steps.text: Persian rule in this land is real. Judah becomes a small province, later called Yehud, under a governor, paying tax to the great king.
claims: Judah becomes a small Persian province, later called Yehud, under a governor, paying tax to the great king.

steps.text: The Bible names two leaders in these years: Sheshbazzar, who is said to have laid a foundation, and Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, with the priest Jeshua.

steps.text: How these two men relate to each other, and whether both belong to the first years of Cyrus, is disputed.

steps.text: The book of Ezra says that the people of the land, including some who claimed to worship the same god, offered to help, and were refused, and then worked to stop the building.

steps.text: That quarrel may remember real tension between those who returned and those who had remained, or between Jerusalem and Samaria. Scholars do not agree how much of Ezra's account is of this time, and how much was shaped later.
claims: How much of Ezra 4 remembers real tension in this period, and how much was shaped later, is disputed.

steps.text: For years, the Bible says, the work on the house of the Lord ceased.
claims: Ezra says the work on the house of the Lord ceased for years.

steps.text: Cyrus dies on campaign, in the north-east. His son Cambyses takes Egypt. The details of Cyrus's death are told in more than one way.

The details of Cyrus's death are told in more than one way.

steps.text: After Cambyses, the empire shakes. Darius, a Persian of another branch of the royal house, takes the throne, and cuts a great inscription on the rock at Behistun, in three languages, to tell how he put down the revolts.

steps.text: The books of Haggai and Zechariah present themselves as words spoken in the second year of Darius, five twenty BC, urging Zerubbabel and the high priest to finish the house of the Lord.

steps.text: A scroll is said to be found at Ecbatana, in Media, and Darius confirms the work. That official correspondence is told only in the book of Ezra.

steps.text: In the sixth year of Darius, five sixteen BC in the usual reckoning, the Bible says the house was finished, and dedicated with joy.
claims: Ezra 6 says the house was finished in the sixth year of Darius, usually reckoned as 516 BC, and dedicated with joy.

steps.text: Of that Second Temple, as it first stood, no certain stone has been identified. Herod would one day rebuild the mount on a far greater scale, and what lies under it is not open to us.

steps.text: Imagine a modest house on the old hill, not the Temple of Solomon as tradition paints it, and not the great courts of later times, but a place where offerings began again.
This is not a new kingdom of David. It is Yehud, a small Persian province, with a governor, a priest, and a tax.
claims: Yehud is a small Persian province, with a governor, a priest, and a tax, not a restored kingdom of David.

steps.text: Coins and seal impressions from a little later name the province and its governors. They do not restore a king.

steps.text: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.
claims: Many of Israel's people are carried off to Assyria. In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of the empire.

steps.text: Then Hezekiah of Judah prepares for war, and Sennacherib of Assyria takes Lachish and shuts the king up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.
claims: Then Hezekiah of Judah prepares for war, and Sennacherib of Assyria takes Lachish and shuts the king up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.

steps.text: The Bible and the Assyrian annals tell two different endings. Jerusalem is not taken, and Judah survives, smaller.
claims: The Bible and the Assyrian annals tell two different endings.
Jerusalem is not taken, and Judah survives, smaller.

steps.text: Sennacherib is later killed by his own son. The city has been spared.
claims: Sennacherib is later killed by his own son. The city has been spared.

steps.text: Then Babylon takes Jerusalem and burns the city. Many are taken east; a remnant remains in the land of Benjamin.
claims: Babylon takes Jerusalem and burns the city.
Many are taken east; a remnant remains in Benjamin.

steps.text: Clay tablets in Babylon name Yaukin, king of Judah, still fed at the emperor's table. The Bible says the Temple was destroyed.
claims: Tablets in Babylon name Yaukin, king of Judah.
The Bible says the Temple was destroyed.

steps.text: The land is not empty, and a generation later a Persian king will take Babylon itself.
claims: The land is not empty, and a generation later a Persian king will take Babylon itself.
